content: An adapted process, also known as a non-anticipating process, is a type of stochastic process that is constrained by the principle that it cannot incorporate or see information from the future. This concept is critical in mathematical finance and probability theory, particularly in the definition of the Itō integral, which requires the integrand to be an adapted process for the integral to be well-defined. To formally define an adapted process, consider the following components: An index set (I) equipped with a total order (leq). Common choices for (I) include (mathbb{N}) (the set of natural numbers), (mathbb{N}_0) (natural numbers including zero), or ([0, +infty)) (non-negative real numbers). A filtration ((mathcal{F}_i)_{i in I}), which is a family of sigma-algebras indexed by (I) and satisfying the property that (mathcal{F}_i subseteq mathcal{F}_j) whenever (i leq j). This filtration represents the evolution of information over time. A measurable space ((S, Sigma)), referred to as the state space, where (S) is the set of possible values the process can take, and (Sigma) is a sigma-algebra on (S). A stochastic process (X: I times Omega to S), which is a collection of random variables indexed by (I). The stochastic process (X) is said to be adapted to the filtration ((mathcal{F}_i)_{i in I}) if, for every (i in I), the random variable (X_i: Omega to S) is measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra ((mathcal{F}_i, Sigma)). In simpler terms, this means that the value of (X_i) at any given time (i) depends only on the information available up to that time, as encoded in (mathcal{F}_i). Example 1: Natural Filtration Consider a stochastic process (X: I times Omega to mathbb{R}), where the state space is the real line (mathbb{R}) equipped with its standard Borel sigma-algebra (the sigma-algebra generated by open subsets of (mathbb{R})). Define the natural filtration ((mathcal{F}_t^X)) of (X), where (mathcal{F}_t^X) is the sigma-algebra generated by the pre-images (X_s^{-1}(B)) for all Borel subsets (B subseteq mathbb{R}) and all times (0 leq s leq t). Intuitively, (mathcal{F}_t^X) contains all the information about the behavior of (X) up to time (t). In this case, the process (X) is automatically adapted to its natural filtration ((mathcal{F}_t^X)), as the filtration is specifically constructed to reflect the information contained in (X) up to each time (t). Example 2: Non-Adapted Process Now, consider a different filtration ((mathcal{F}_t)) defined as follows: For (0 leq t < 1), let (mathcal{F}_t) be the trivial sigma-algebra ({emptyset, Omega}), which contains no meaningful information about the process. For (1 leq t leq 2), let (mathcal{F}_t = mathcal{F}_t^X), the natural filtration of (X). In this setup, any stochastic process (X) that is not constant on the interval ([0, 1)) will fail to be adapted to the filtration ((mathcal{F}_t)). This is because, for (0 leq t < 1), the trivial sigma-algebra ({emptyset, Omega}) only allows measurable functions that are constant. If (X) is non-constant during this time interval, it uses information that is not available in the trivial sigma-algebra, thereby violating the condition of being adapted. This illustrates how a process can fail to be adapted when it relies on information from a more refined sigma-algebra that becomes available only in the future.
